opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think what's really interesting right now is that we've stumbled into this situation where a lot of the most capable models of the world we have were trained mostly, or at least first, on text. And that's a strange place to start if you think about how people learn. Kids are grounded in perception and action long before they're reading anything. So there's a real question about what you can actually learn about the world from language alone, and then what changes when you bolt vision or other modalities onto that.

One thing I find fascinating is that the answer to "what can you learn from text?" seems to be "a surprising amount." There's a lot of structure about the physical world, about spatial relations, about color, about how objects behave, that gets reflected in how people talk. So when you probe these language models, you sometimes find representations that line up in nontrivial ways with perceptual structure, even though the model has never seen an image. And then when you train multimodal models, there's this question of whether the visual side is really contributing new information, or whether language is doing most of the organizing work and the vision encoder is just getting mapped into a space that text already carved out.

I'm also interested in the other direction: language as a kind of supervision signal that tells you which distinctions matter. The world has infinitely many features you could attend to, and language is a compressed record of the ones humans have found useful enough to name. So training with language may be less about adding facts and more about imposing a particular abstraction, a set of categories and compositional structure that makes generalization easier. Some of our work on learning with latent language, using natural language descriptions as an intermediate representation for policies or classifiers, is trying to get at exactly that.

And finally there's the cautionary side. If language shapes these representations so heavily, then the models inherit the gaps and biases of what people bother to say. We rarely state the obvious, so things like typical sizes of objects or everyday physical regularities can be underrepresented. Understanding where language helps and where it quietly misleads the model seems like one of the most important open questions for building systems that actually model the world rather than just modeling talk about it.

r001.rationale: The response says language can impose categories and abstractions, but it does not ask how language shapes the units into which multimodal models segment perceptual input.

r002.rationale: The response contrasts models’ text-first training with how children learn, but it does not call for comparing models’ organization of the world with humans’ actual organization rather than researchers’ assumptions.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the thing that really draws me in is that language is sort of a strange kind of training signal. If you're training a vision model on images alone, the structure it discovers is whatever structure happens to be useful for the task, maybe reconstructing pixels or distinguishing one image from another. But the moment you start pairing those images with captions, or with instructions, or with questions, you're injecting a very particular set of human abstractions into the problem. Language has already done a lot of work carving the world up into objects, into categories, into relations, into events, and it's done that in ways that reflect what people care about rather than what's statistically salient in the pixels.

So one question I find really interesting is: how much of the conceptual structure we see in these models is coming from the visual data itself, and how much is being imposed by the language? There's a long-running debate in cognitive science about linguistic relativity, about whether the language you speak shapes the way you perceive color or space or time, and in some sense multimodal models give us a very clean experimental setup for versions of that question. We can hold the images fixed, vary the language, and look at what happens to the representations.

And then the flip side, which is maybe more practical, is that language gives us a handle on these representations. If a model's internal features align with words and phrases, then we can ask the model to describe what it's attending to, we can intervene by editing text, we can probe for concepts by name. That's not something you get for free from a purely visual system. So part of what I'm interested in is whether we can actually exploit that, whether the fact that these models have been trained to ground language gives us a kind of interface for understanding and controlling what they've learned.

What I don't think we fully understand yet is where that alignment breaks down. There are plenty of visual concepts that don't have good names, and there are plenty of linguistic distinctions that don't correspond to anything perceptually stable. So the interesting cases are the ones where language and perception pull in different directions, and seeing which one wins tells you something about what the model is actually doing.

r001.rationale: The response asks how much conceptual structure comes from language and proposes varying language while holding images fixed; its examples of objects, categories, relations, and events convey how language shapes perceptual grouping.

r002.rationale: The response mentions human perception and linguistic relativity, but does not call for comparing models’ organization with how humans actually organize the world rather than with researchers’ assumptions.

astra-6.text:
One thing that interests me is that language gives us a way to learn about the world without directly experiencing everything we want to understand. You can learn something by looking at it or interacting with it, but you can also learn because somebody tells you about it. And those sources of information are complementary.

So when we train a model on images and language together, I want to understand what the language is actually doing to its representation. Is it just giving names to distinctions the model could already discover visually? Or is it helping the model identify relationships and abstractions that would be difficult to learn from images alone?

There’s also an interesting tension there, because language is selective. A description doesn’t capture everything in an image; it captures what somebody thought was worth mentioning. That can be a very useful learning signal, but it can also leave things out. Understanding how that selectivity shapes what models learn—and what they fail to learn—is a big part of what makes this interesting to me.

r001.rationale: The response asks how language shapes a model’s representation and learned distinctions, relationships, and abstractions, but does not ask how it segments perceptual input into units.

r002.rationale: The response does not compare models’ organization of the world with how humans organize it, or distinguish that comparison from researchers’ assumptions.

sol-6.1.text:
One thing I find really interesting is that language gives us a way to learn about the world without directly experiencing everything we want to understand. You can learn something by looking at it or interacting with it, but you can also learn from somebody telling you about it. And those sources of information are complementary.

So, for multimodal models, the question is how those sources fit together. If a model learns from both images and text, does language help it discover concepts that would be difficult to learn from images alone? Does it change which distinctions the model pays attention to, or how it generalizes to situations it hasn’t seen before?

There’s also a tension there, because language is a very selective description of the world. We talk about some things and leave a lot unsaid. I’m interested in when that selectivity provides useful structure for learning, and when it leads a model to miss something that’s right there in the visual evidence.

r001.rationale: The response asks whether language changes the distinctions a model attends to, but does not ask how it segments perceptual input into units.
